entries.title: Pep Guardiola calls on world to ‘disobey horror’ over Gaza and praises BDS
entries.summary: Football icon says it is more urgent than ever to demand an end to Israel's 'apartheid, colonialism and occupation'.
entries.content:
Football icon says it is more urgent than ever to demand an end to Israel’s ‘apartheid, colonialism and occupation’.

Pep Guardiola has called on the world to “disobey horror” over Israel’s genocide in Gaza, in an address to Boycott Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) activists exclusively shared with Al Jazeera.

The footballing icon made the remarks to the BDS@20 European conference in Barcelona last week, saying the international demand for an end to “apartheid, colonialism and occupation” was more urgent than ever.

“The world after Gaza demands that we disobey horror,” Guardiola said, in an address that drew on Barcelona’s history of resistance, the writings of Palestinian intellectuals and the international campaign against apartheid in South Africa.

The former Manchester City, Bayern Munich and Barcelona coach urged people across different sectors of society to consider their responsibility to act, “knowing that no system of apartheid ends on its own and that silence will save none of us”.

“Whenever I am asked what sport can do, I think it can do a great deal, and more,” Guardiola said. “The same question applies to every field. What can culture do? What can science do? What can international politics do?”

In an address delivered to a packed audience at Barcelona’s Casino l’Alianca del Poblenou, Guardiola thanked the BDS movement for “all you have done, all you are doing and all you will do”.

The conference brought together activists, academics, artists, trade unionists and campaigners from across Europe and beyond to discuss the next phase of international solidarity with Palestine.

Among those attending was Rebecca O’Keeffe of Irish Sport for Palestine, whose work has included the Stop The Game campaign, calling on the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) to withdraw from fixtures against Israel.

O’Keeffe said Guardiola’s willingness to use his global platform was particularly significant in a sporting world where athletes can face pushback for speaking out.

“People like Pep Guardiola, people with such a huge platform … the reach it can have is invaluable,” she told Al Jazeera.

Reflecting on the scale of the devastation in Gaza, Guardiola said the international community’s demands had become more urgent.

“Today our immediate, shared demand is to stop a genocide, break a siege and put an end to forced displacement,” he said.

“Every gesture matters because every life counts.”

The Spanish coach drew a parallel between the Palestinian struggle and Barcelona’s own history, recalling the city’s bombardment during the Spanish Civil War and the network of more than 1,300 underground shelters built to protect civilians.

“Barcelona, like so many cities elsewhere, also came under bombardment beneath a leaden sky, in the middle of a war,” he said.

He described the city as one that had consistently stood in solidarity with Palestine, welcoming the decision to host the European BDS conference.

For O’Keeffe, the influence of figures such as Guardiola is part of a wider effort to mobilise people from across the sporting world.

“Having Irish Sport for Palestine led and informed by people within the sporting community, is our greatest strength and greatest asset. The power of the athlete’s voice is incredible,” she said.

In closing his remarks, Guardiola moved beyond sport and drew on the writings of Palestinian poet Mahmoud Darwish and intellectual Edward Said, recalling an exchange between the two in which Said described the future of Palestinian liberation as “the impossible”.

When Darwish asked whether the impossible was far away, Said replied: “One generation away.”

“You are that generation now,” Guardiola told delegates.

He concluded by invoking Handala, the famous Palestinian cartoon character created by Naji al-Ali, whose back is always turned to the viewer until Palestinians are able to return home.

“May the seeds of solidarity continue to sprout. May Handala come home soon,” Guardiola said.

“End colonialism, end occupation, end apartheid.”

entries.title: Qatari, Egyptian leaders discuss Gaza ‘ceasefire’ and regional security
entries.summary: Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani is in Cairo for an official visit aimed at further strengthening bilateral relations.
entries.content:
Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani is in Cairo for an official visit aimed at further strengthening bilateral relations.

Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi have discussed regional tensions and efforts to implement the Gaza “ceasefire” during talks in Cairo.

El-Sisi received the emir on Thursday at Cairo International Airport upon his arrival for an official visit at the Egyptian president’s invitation. After a reception at the presidential palace, the talks began.

Sheikh Tamim’s visit was aimed at further strengthening bilateral relations across various sectors, including investment and energy, as well as coordinating diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions and bolster regional security, Qatar said.

“Today, I discussed with my brother, President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, the latest developments in the region and the importance of continuing consultations and coordinating joint efforts to address current challenges, in a way that helps safeguard our region’s security and stability and fulfil its peoples’ aspirations for peace and prosperity,” Sheikh Tamim said on X after the meeting.

The two leaders discussed efforts to promote regional stability, Egyptian presidential spokesman Mohamed el-Shenawy said in a statement.

They stressed the importance of “intensifying regional and international efforts to prioritise political solutions and dialogue and prevent tensions from widening”, warning of “serious consequences for regional and international security and stability”, the statement added.

The talks also addressed developments in Palestine with el-Sisi outlining Egypt’s efforts to implement the Gaza “ceasefire”.

The Egyptian leader emphasised the need for all parties to uphold the agreement, ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip and begin recovery and reconstruction programmes without delay.

Qatar’s Emiri Diwan said in a statement that the two leaders exchanged views on the latest regional and international developments, “particularly the situation in the Gaza Strip and joint mediation efforts to solidify the ceasefire”.

The Egyptian statement said el-Sisi also reaffirmed Egypt’s “full support for the security of Qatar and other Gulf states”, stressing that “the security of the Gulf is an integral part of Egypt’s national security”.

It also said the two leaders discussed ways to strengthen economic ties and cooperation in areas of mutual interest and they agreed to continue “intensifying political consultations and coordination”.

The meeting was also attended by Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani and other senior officials from both countries.

entries.title: US judge blocks Trump’s FCC attempt to target Disney’s ABC stations
entries.summary: The judge said the FCC chair has taken US President Donald Trump's rhetoric ‌‌as his 'marching orders'.
entries.content:
The judge said the FCC chair has taken US President Donald Trump’s rhetoric ‌‌as his ‘marching orders’.

A United States judge has barred the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from putting the licences of eight Walt Disney-owned ABC TV stations up for early review, a blow ⁠⁠to President Donald Trump’s efforts to rein in US media companies.

US District Judge Loren AliKhan, in Washington, DC, granted Disney’s request for a preliminary injunction on Wednesday. The injunction barred the FCC from holding a hearing on the licences, a step that could have led to their revocation and forced the stations off ⁠⁠the air.

“This is not a close case,” AliKhan wrote, saying the FCC appeared to be carrying out a retaliatory campaign, driven by Trump, that threatened the broadcaster’s free-speech rights.

AliKhan, who was nominated by former President Joe Biden, said ABC had detailed “a campaign of retaliation against them in response to their exercise of their First Amendment rights,” which on its own is an ‘irreparable injury’”.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr, whom Trump named to the position in January 2025, “has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders”, the judge added.

A spokesperson for ABC News said, “Today’s decision is an important victory for ⁠⁠the First Amendment.”

Carr ordered reviews of licences ‌for the eight stations in April, a day after Trump urged ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, even though the renewals were not due to be considered until October 2028 at the earliest. The FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years before April.

Disney and ABC sued the FCC in August to block the early review of the stations in Los Angeles, Chicago, New York and other cities, arguing that the Trump administration was trying to punish the network over broadcast content in violation of the US Constitution.

In response to AliKhan’s decision, an FCC spokesperson has said that the granting of the injunction was “wrong on the facts and ⁠⁠wrong on the law — as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear.”

They added, “We will continue to use our lawful ⁠⁠authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations.”

Trump has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop comedy or news programmes that he dislikes or that have been critical of him or his administration.

Broadcast stations need FCC licences to use public airwaves. While licence revocations are extremely rare, critics said that the risk of losing a licence could have a ⁠⁠chilling effect on a broadcaster and raise concerns about government interference.

Trump has waged aggressive ⁠⁠attacks on the news media, and the latest move follows a two-year-long battle between Trump and Disney.

In July, Trump repeated a call for ABC stations to lose their licences because the network refused to air a prime-time speech he gave that said US elections are vulnerable to fraud.

In reacting to the judicial decision, Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez said the ruling “brings ‌‌badly needed accountability to a commission and an administration that have politicised the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control”.

The FCC is also investigating ABC daytime talk show “The View,” which discusses US politics, after saying it may be subject to federal rules requiring broadcasters ‌‌to ‌‌provide equal-time opportunities to political candidates.

Disney previously said that as a result of that investigation, the programme did not invite any political candidates to appear before the November midterm elections, and the broadcaster cited the FCC’s “pressure campaign”.

entries.title: Andalusia offers a glimpse of Spain’s future as the far right gains ground
entries.summary: Ahead of Sunday's election, Andalusia signals Vox’s rise as immigration and right-wing alliances reshape politics.
entries.content:
Ahead of Sunday’s election, Andalusia signals Vox’s rise as immigration and right-wing alliances reshape Spain’s politics.

Andalusia, Spain – Surrounded by shelves heaving with canned goods and cured meats, the owners of a family-run grocery store are locked in a debate about Spain’s upcoming elections.

All politicians are “liars”, proclaims 32-year-old Antonio Cerezo, announcing he will cast a blank ballot. His cousin, Patricia Nicolas Cerezo, 43, is less certain, riddled with doubt about who to support.

As for her 18-year-old son, first-time voter Alfonso Duque, the only choice is the far-right Vox party: “It can’t get worse than this”.

The one thing that the family in the small village of Rioja seems to agree on is that Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s socialists must go.

A former socialist bastion, the southern region’s political landscape has changed. Since May’s regional election, it has been governed by a coalition of the conservative People’s Party (PP) and Vox, once a fringe party that has drawn support by championing migrant deportations and tapping into a wider wave of far-right, anti-establishment support across Europe.

Ahead of Sunday’s snap vote, observers say Andalusia’s political dynamics could offer a glimpse of what might come next nationally.

That arrangement could soon be tested at the national level.

Opinion polls put the PP first, followed by Sanchez’s Socialists (PSOE), with Vox third.

The PP is projected to fall short of an outright majority, but together the two right-wing parties are expected to have enough seats to govern.

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo has indicated that he would prefer to lead a minority government with Vox’s backing in parliament, while leaving open the possibility of a coalition like the one in Andalusia.

Tucked away between rows of greenhouses and arid mountains in the southern region of Andalusia, Rioja is home to about 1,600 people.

Overlooking the plains framing the quaint village is a giant silhouette of a bull. For much of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship, this area remained poor and largely agricultural.

As machines took over more of the work in the fields, many Andalusians left for jobs in industrial centres such as Barcelona and Madrid. In the mid-seventies, the Socialists found fertile ground in a society that had long felt marginalised and neglected.

In 1982, the PSOE won an absolute majority in Andalusia’s first regional election, beginning a stretch in power that lasted more than three decades.

‘The PP opened the door to the far-right’

But by 2018, the Socialists’ hold on the southern region was starting to crack.

A series of corruption scandals tarnished the party’s image, benefitting the PP. The PSOE still came first in that year’s regional election, but the conservatives took power with the backing of the liberal Ciudadanos and Vox.

It was a turning point.

“For the first time, the PP opened the door to the far-right to be able to govern – that created a precedent for everything that happens today nationwide,” said Bosco Govantes, political science associate professor at Sevilla’s Universidad Pablo de Olavide. “Before, there was a red line, a stigma, over collaborating with the far right. But that move in Andalusia kicked off the normalisation of Vox’s narrative.”

The party was founded in 2013 when a group of ultraconservatives, led by Santiago Abascal, broke up with the conservatives they accused of being too indulgent towards Catalan separatists.

Vox at first struggled to get into the political mainstream, but entered Andalusia’s regional parliament in 2018.

Once the Catalan issue faded from the national debate, the party shifted its focus to migration.

Abascal accuses Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people” as the Socialist government adopted an open-door policy and legalised undocumented migrants who had worked in Spain for years.

Since the start of Sanchez’s rule to last year, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, official figures show. He takes pride in the policy, as Spain’s GDP grew under his tenure.

Vox, the likely kingmaker that is expected to increase its vote share more than any other party compared with the 2023 elections, wants to reverse those policies.

Some observers say the conservative party has had to harden its discourse, such as calling for stricter measures against migrants, to stop haemorrhaging voters to its right.

Polling by Ipsos suggested up to 20 percent of Spaniards who voted for the PP in the 2023 elections intended to vote for Vox on Sunday.

Sanchez has pitched the election as a battle between progress and regression, warning that PP and Vox “only agree when it comes to cutting back rights”.

But that argument falls flat in parts of Andalusia, where some do not fear a Vox-PP deal.

“I don’t mind if Vox is in government,” said Rosaria, a 69-year-old retired housewife, while adjusting her white scarf with a red floral pattern. “The PP will keep them in check. It’s a party with vision and structure”.

Sanchez warns that Vox wants to roll back women’s rights.

The issue of gender violence divides the two parties.

Last year, the PP backed the renewal of Spain’s cross-party pact on gender-based violence.

Vox wants to repeal the 2004 gender-based violence law, which protects women from abuse by current or former partners. The party argues that the law discriminates against men and wants to replace it with legislation covering domestic violence regardless of the victim’s sex.

At an event against gender-based violence, Rioja’s PP mayor Olga Maria Gonzalez Jurado was asked how the two parties were getting on in government in Andalusia.

“I think it’s going well,” she said, but she deflected questions on whether the PP had hardened its stance on immigration to keep up with Vox.

In Andalusia, the two parties have been pushing for stricter housing rules for non-Spanish applicants.

Councils can already give people who live or work locally priority for subsidised housing, regardless of nationality. Last month, the two parties backed a non-binding motion urging Madrid to give Spanish citizens priority for subsidised housing and housing aid. Their regional coalition deal also pledges to give people with longstanding ties to Andalusia or Spain priority for public benefits and social housing.

In other regions, the two parties’ cooperation has reached classrooms and places of worship. Aragon dropped a school programme teaching Arabic and Moroccan culture this year and Andalusia is due to follow in 2027.

In the Murcia town of Jumilla, Muslims held Eid al-Fitr prayers in a car park after PP and Vox backed restrictions on the use of municipal sports facilities. The restrictions have drawn criticism over their impact on Muslim religious gatherings.

In Valencia, the parties backed a rule requiring meat served in school canteens to come from animals stunned before slaughter, which still allows halal meals that meet the requirement. In the Balearic Islands, they voted to send Spain’s Congress a bill to ban the burqa [full-face veils sometimes worn by Muslim women that hide the entire face, including eyes] and niqab [similar, but the eyes are visible] in public spaces.

Vox has called for the deportation of foreigners it says, among other grounds, also live on public benefits. This measure – to remove someone with a valid right to stay – has no equivalent in Europe.

The party’s policies have left migrants on edge.

Yudy Ramirez is from Colombia and entered Spain four years ago. For years, took care of her child while juggling two jobs as an in-house caregiver and fruit picker at a greenhouse in Almeria for five euros per hour.

In June, the 49-year-old finally received legal papers.

“Many of us are scared, because returning is not in the plans at the moment,” she said.

Still, not all migrants are targeted in the same way.

Vox’s rhetoric has an ethno-racial undertone which looks at Spanish-speaking foreigners coming from Latin America in more favourable terms as they belong to an Iberosphere which connects far-right movements in the Latin world whose centre is occupied by Vox.

Andalusia heavily relies on foreign workers for its greenhouses.

According to Govantes, the issue is not with migrants working in Spain but with them being recognised for their rights. The PSOE’s regularisation, he said, forced owners to make legal contracts, pay social security and provide benefits.

“Migrants’ work has always been tolerated as long as it was invisible and illegal. As they became visible and legal, they were accused of robbing Spanish people of jobs,” he said.

entries.title: Why is Italy angry with Ukraine for striking Russian ships off Libya?
entries.summary: Analysts say Rome fears instability in Libya could hurt its energy interests and efforts to curb irregular migration.
entries.content:
Analysts say Rome fears instability in Libya could hurt its energy interests and efforts to curb irregular migration.

Italy has denounced Ukraine for carrying out attacks against Russian vessels in Libyan waters, saying it was wrong to “violate Libya’s sovereignty”.

Rome’s rebuke marks a crack in its relationship with Ukraine, which Italy has largely supported since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, including with military assistance.

It coincides with growing concern about the involvement of foreign powers in a divided Libya, as well as the risk of other nations being drawn into the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

So why has Italy weighed in now, and what makes Libya so strategically important to Rome?

Why did Ukraine carry out an attack in Libyan waters?

Kyiv claimed it sank a Russian warship and struck a cargo vessel transporting military equipment off Libya’s coast on Sunday night. The attack on the warship at Benghazi port in eastern Libya killed two naval officers of the self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), according to Libya’s eastern-based forces.

Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the vessels as legitimate targets, arguing Kyiv had the legal right to defend itself against “Russian aggression”.

He stressed that Ukraine’s actions were “not intended to harm Libya or its people” and that Kyiv respects Libya’s territorial integrity.

“Ukraine is not ‘dragging’ anyone into the war or ‘transferring’ the war anywhere,” Sybiha said in a statement on Telegram.

How did Libya react?

Musa al-Koni, the vice president of Libya’s Tripoli-based Presidential Council, called the attack “a declaration of war against the Libyan state”.

Libyan authorities “hold the Ukrainian side fully responsible for these terrorist acts”, he added.

The LNA, a rival power that controls eastern and southern parts of Libya and maintains close relations with Russia, promised to retaliate against the Ukrainian attack “at the appropriate time and place, and by the appropriate means”.

Libya is divided between the UN-recognised government in Tripoli and a parallel administration based in Benghazi, backed by the LNA and its renegade commander, Khalifa Haftar.

How did Italy react?

Italy’s Foreign Minister ⁠⁠Antonio Tajani said it was a mistake for Ukraine to “violate Libya’s sovereignty” and that Rome, which has a small military presence in Libya, had received no prior notice of the operation.

“Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv’s intentions to strike in Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port,” Tajani told Italy’s Corriere della Sera newspaper.

Italy’s far-right League party, which is a member of the coalition government, also criticised the attack, saying it risked sowing instability inside Libya.

The comments expose a rare rift with Ukraine, which Italy has largely supported in the war against Russia. Italy has provided Ukraine with more than 3 billion euros ($3.29bn) worth of military aid, according to data from the Kiel Institute think tank, while also backing sweeping sanctions against Russia.

However, there has been division within Italy’s government over further aid to Ukraine, with Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, who heads the League party, opposing more weapons shipments or funding.

Matteo Villa, a senior research fellow at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI), told Al Jazeera that Ukraine’s recent attack off Libya is likely to deepen these domestic tensions.

It “gives Salvini an opportunity to strengthen his case, questioning whether Western military assistance risks enabling Ukraine to pursue objectives that run counter to Italy’s own national interests”, said Villa.

What relationship does Italy have with Libya?

Italy, whose southern islands lie 300km (186 miles) across the Mediterranean from the Libyan coast, has spent years building ties with rival factions in western and eastern Libya.

“Over the past few years, Rome has shifted from almost complete support for the UN-backed Western government in Libya towards building working relationships with the Haftar-controlled East as well,” said Villa.

Italy has also for years helped provide funding, equipment and training for Libya’s maritime authorities, despite reports of migrants being abused and tortured in Libyan custody.

The aim has been to curb irregular migration from Libya to Italy, one of the most perilous and contested Europe-bound routes.

Alessia Melcangi, a nonresident senior fellow with the North Africa Program at the Atlantic Council’s Rafik Hariri Center and Middle East Programs, said Italy’s condemnation of Ukraine partly serves as a form of “damage control” to help Rome balance its competing geopolitical interests.

“Rome needs to demonstrate that its relationships with Kyiv, Tripoli and Benghazi give it meaningful influence over developments affecting its security,” Melcangi told Al Jazeera. “Otherwise, perceptions of exclusion or ambiguity could cause lasting diplomatic damage.”

Why is Italy concerned about conflict spilling into Libya?

Villa said Rome’s concerns are fuelled by its geographical proximity to Libya, as well as its economic and strategic interests there, specifically in terms of energy and “migration control”.

“Last year, Libya accounted for roughly a quarter of Italy’s crude oil imports, making it its largest supplier, and the country is by far the main departure point for migrants reaching Italy by sea,” said Villa.

Aldo Liga, a research fellow at the Middle East and North Africa Centre at ISPI, told Al Jazeera that potential escalation that further destabilises Libya would “threaten the security of trade routes and energy flows”, creating a volatile security situation in the Strait of Sicily.

“Instability in Libya is perceived as a direct threat to Italy’s national interests,” he said.

In his interview with Corriere della Sera, Foreign Minister Tajani cited the presence of the Italian military and Italian petroleum company Eni in Libya as being among his concerns about the Ukrainian intervention.

“What happened is worrying,” Tajani said, referring to the Ukrainian attack. “The war between Russia and Ukraine must be prevented from widening, avoiding new outbreaks from occurring.”

entries.title: UN ruling disputes Israeli allegations used to dismiss UNRWA Gaza staff
entries.summary: Tribunal raises questions about the credibility of UNRWA's decision to dismiss its staff without substantiated evidence.
entries.content:
Tribunal raises questions about the credibility of UNRWA’s decision to dismiss its staff without substantiated evidence.

A United Nations tribunal has cast doubt on evidence used by UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, to dismiss staff in 2024, finding that the decision was based almost entirely on unsubstantiated allegations by the Israeli government.

UNRWA dismissed nine Palestinian employees in January 2024 after allegations by Israel that they had participated in the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.

The UNRWA Dispute Tribunal, an impartial tribunal within the UN, noted that the UN’s internal investigation did not include testimonies from the 19 staff members whom Israel accused of involvement in the attacks, according to the judgement seen by Al Jazeera on Thursday.

The judgement said “safety and security concerns” meant that the UN Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS) “was not able to interview the 19 staff members and afford them usual due process to respond to the allegations”.

The tribunal also said the allegations against the workers were “based almost entirely on information in Israel’s possession”.

“That information has remained in the custody of Israeli authorities and they alone have remained privy as to exactly how it was collected, by whom, when, and where,” it said.

The tribunal also expressed doubts over telephone conversations and messages that Israel claimed to have intercepted and presented as evidence of the staff members’ involvement in the attacks, including with someone “identified by Israeli officials as a Hamas operative”.

“OIOS did not confirm in the investigation report that it was satisfied that the caller was a Hamas operative or that the ‘user’ of the receiving phone was the Applicant,” the judgement said.

It added that one of the Israeli claims of an alleged intercepted phone call between a Hamas operative and a UNRWA staff member was with a duplicated SIM card, which is common in Gaza. “It was determined that the comments made in intercepted calls related to that SIM card were not made by the UNRWA staff member as initially alleged,” the judgement said.

The tribunal’s ruling, dated November 11, found that UNRWA had failed to produce evidence supporting its decision to dismiss one of the nine employees, identified as Abu Awad.

The tribunal described Israeli evidence as unsupported and of “limited evidentiary value and reliability” and awarded Awad a year’s pay and $5,000 in compensation for “moral damages”.

The ruling raises questions about the credibility of the decision by UNRWA, the main humanitarian organisation operating in Gaza, to dismiss its Palestinian staff on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the attacks committed by Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups.

In January 2024 after consulting UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, former UNRWA Commissioner General Philippe Lazzarini decided that the agency would terminate the contracts of nine staff members.

Their termination letters informed them that the allegations against them were “very serious and credible”.

The dismissal decisions were confirmed after a UN investigation that concluded they were likely to have been involved in the October 7 attacks.

Reports have suggested that Lazzarini and Guterres likely made this decision in the hopes that appeasing Israel and its allies would allow humanitarian work in Gaza to continue.

But UNRWA still experienced critical funding cuts from donors. About 600 of its staff members were laid off, salaries in Gaza were cut by 20 percent and aid access remained blocked by Israel amid a worsening humanitarian crisis in the enclave.

entries.title: Can Trump continue with Iran war despite funding restrictions?
entries.summary: A Congress budget bill could serve as a pressure tactic on Trump to end the war but could also trigger a shutdown.
entries.content:
A Congress budget bill could serve as a pressure tactic on Trump to end the war but could also cause a government shutdown.

As US Democrats prepare to assume control of both houses of Congress in January following victory in the midterm elections, the issue of ending the war on Iran is back in sharp focus.

Until now, efforts by the Democrats to end the nine-month war that has led to soaring food and fuel prices have failed. Now, they fear that as Iran and the US remain deadlocked in the Strait of Hormuz, President Donald Trump could opt to restart strikes on Iran, triggering likely retaliatory attacks across the Gulf.

A new budget bill is in the works and could serve as a pressure tactic on Trump if it limits funding for the war. So what are Trump’s options now?

Here’s what we know:

Can Democrats use the funding bill to end the war on Iran?

With federal funding set to expire on December 11 , Republican and Democratic legislators are negotiating to reach a bipartisan agreement for the next round of funding. This must be agreed to avoid a government shutdown and ensure federal agencies, services and military operations during the Iran war can continue.

Last week, Congress representatives Yassamin Ansari and Ro Khanna called on Democratic colleagues to use the deadline to pressure the White House to end the war.

“Ahead of the December 11 government funding deadline, Congress faces the task of approving a funding package to maintain government operations,” their statement read.

“Congress must use its constitutional power of the purse to ensure that not another cent of taxpayer money goes towards prolonging this war. We will oppose any funding package that does not explicitly prohibit funds from being used for offensive operations in Iran. Passing such a measure would defy the demands of Americans who want this war to end – now.”

According to the most recent polling from Reuters/Ipsos, 71 percent of Americans say they want the new Congress to end the Iran war.

Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London, said the bill is “potentially the first serious institutional constraint on Trump’s freedom to wage war against Iran”.

“Until now, Washington’s military strategy has been largely insulated from congressional opposition. The Democrats are trying to change that by making continued offensive operations conditional on congressional authorisation,” Krieg told Al Jazeera.

What is the main obstacle?

Politicians are divided about whether bringing an end to the war now is worth the risk of a government shutdown. Last year, the US government shut down for 43 days from 1 October to 12 November, because Congress failed to pass funding for 2026.

“The American people don’t need another government shutdown,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters this week. “I think that would be a colossal mistake and a real disservice to the people of this country.”

Senator Peter Welch, a Vermont Democrat, told Reuters that the “big obstacle is that we don’t want to fund the war, we don’t want to shut down, how do you solve that?”

A new bipartisan funding package would require 60 votes in the 100-seat Senate, which until January has 53 Republicans and 45 Democrats. When the new class of senators is sworn in during January, this will flip to 44 Republicans and 54 Democrats.

Another issue is that it may not be that easy to end the war, regardless of the funding issue.

Krieg said: “Restricting offensive spending does not end the war. The American blockade remains in place, Iran continues challenging maritime navigation, and neither side has resolved the fundamental disputes over nuclear inspections, sanctions and Hormuz. The legislation is still a proposal, and its effectiveness will depend on the final wording and whether Trump signs it,” he added.

Could Trump veto a bill that cuts all military spending?

Yes.

While the Democrats won big in the midterms, Trump still retains executive authority enshrined in the Constitution, which states that the president can reject legislation passed by Congress.

A presidential veto can only be overturned by a two-thirds majority in both houses of Congress, something the Democrats do not have the numbers to muster without significant Republican support.

Trump’s presidential veto could be a double-edged sword when it comes to military funding. If he uses it to block a bill denying him funding for the war, paycheques for military personnel would also be blocked as a result of a government shutdown.

Another scenario is that the military retains funding for defensive purposes, which could ultimately continue the war and the ongoing naval blockade of Iran’s ports.

What happens if a Democrat bill isn’t vetoed? Would that end the war?

According to Krieg, even if a new finance bill were to block more funding for the Iran war, Trump could continue military operations with existing resources for “some time”.

“The Pentagon has considerable operational capacity in theatre and the absence of additional funding does not immediately prevent the president from ordering another round of strikes.”

He explained that there is, however, an important difference between having the military capability to escalate a conflict and “having the financial resources to sustain another prolonged campaign”.

“American expenditure is already approaching $50bn, while shortages of precision munitions and air-defence interceptors are becoming an increasingly serious concern. The decisive question is whether Congress simply refuses additional funding or explicitly prohibits offensive operations using money already appropriated,” he said.

Is there a precedent for Congress using funding to end wars?

Yes.

During the Vietnam War, Congress passed a resolution in 1964 that granted then-President Lyndon B Johnson the authority to send troops to Southeast Asia without declaring war. However, as the war dragged on and troop morale tanked, the war grew increasingly unpopular.

In 1973, Congress repealed the resolution and ordered forces to withdraw.

Less successfully, in 2007, the Democrats tried repeatedly to end the Iraq War and linked a troop withdrawal timetable to a funding bill.

However, then-President George Bush vetoed the bill, which led to Democrats and Republicans going back and forth over it.

Eventually, the Democrats backed down and withdrew the troop withdrawal condition from the bill.

According to Krieg, the strongest tool the Democrats have in ending the Iran war now is their ability to withhold funding.

“The 11 December funding deadline gives Democrats leverage to negotiate restrictions before they assume control of Congress in January. The emerging discussion about replenishing US munitions stockpiles in exchange for restrictions on offensive operations is particularly important,” he said.

“However, Trump retains his veto, so Democratic majorities alone cannot guarantee that new restrictions become law. Ultimately, I think the greatest consequence of congressional intervention could be to accelerate the search for a negotiated settlement.”

entries.title: How an oil feud is deepening rift between Baghdad and Iraq’s Kurdish region
entries.summary: Prime Minister al-Zaidi's move to take control of border crossings and oilfields has drawn a sharp response from Erbil.
entries.content:
Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s move to take control of border crossings and oilfields has drawn a sharp response from Erbil.

Iraq’s federal government and the semi-autonomous Kurdish region are locked in their sharpest confrontation in years over who controls the country’s oil, its border crossings and the revenues that flow from them.

The crisis escalated this week. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered federal authorities to take over all border crossings in the northern Kurdish region, close unofficial crossings used for smuggling, and seize control of oilfields in disputed provinces held by Kurdish security forces. Within 24 hours, Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court had issued a ruling backing Baghdad’s powers.

The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) has called the measures a violation of the constitution and accused Baghdad of trying to return Iraq to centralisation. On Wednesday, as reports spread that army units were heading north, the government in Baghdad insisted it had no plans to send troops into the region.

Here is what we know about the dispute, and where it could be headed.

What are the tensions about?

On the surface, the dispute is about oil smuggling.

On Tuesday, al-Zaidi ordered the Border Ports Authority to take over all crossings into the Kurdish region and directed the closure of all unofficial crossings. He told the energy police to secure all oilfields. He also ordered the federal Oil Ministry to take over the management of fields in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Salahuddin and Diyala provinces.

Those provinces lie in a belt of territory that both Baghdad and Erbil claim. The 2005 constitution set out a process under Article 140 to settle their status, but it was never completed.

Kirkuk, home to some of Iraq’s largest oilfields, has been the most bitterly contested. Kurdish forces took control of the city in 2014 after the Iraqi army withdrew from conflict with ISIL (ISIS). Federal forces retook it in October 2017, after the Kurdish region held an independence referendum which Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court later declared unconstitutional and void.

Al Jazeera correspondent Suhaib al-Asa has reported that the oil sites named in this week’s order are, in practice, outside the semi-autonomous Kurdish region but still under the control of its security forces.

The court ruling raised the stakes further. In an interpretive decision, the Federal Supreme Court affirmed the federal government’s authority to secure Iraq’s international borders and deploy the armed forces across all Iraqi territory. The court said federal authorities could supervise border crossings, including those in the Kurdish region. It also confirmed Baghdad’s power to oversee the production and export of oil and gas, as well as oil and non-oil revenues.

Both sides have framed the dispute as a constitutional battle, said Tallha Abdulrazaq, an independent international security and defence consultant based in the United Kingdom. Baghdad cites federal authority over national wealth and borders under Articles 110 and 112, while Erbil invokes shared customs administration and regional autonomy under Article 114.

“Paradoxically, both sides are right,” Abdulrazaq told Al Jazeera. “Since its adoption in 2005, Iraq’s constitution has contained contradictory and ambiguous provisions on oil and border management, making it a recurring recipe for political chaos.”

What has the Iraqi government said?

Baghdad presents its measures as a campaign against corruption and smuggling, not a move against the Kurds.

“National sovereignty is indivisible,” said al-Zaidi, who is also commander-in-chief of the armed forces. He described protecting Iraq’s wealth as “a battle for existence” in which the state would put an end to all forms of smuggling.

The orders follow an investigation into smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company. Al-Zaidi also dismissed eight security and administrative officials, including the head of the Border Ports Authority, Kirkuk’s operations commander and the province’s police chief.

Government spokesperson Haidar al-Aboudi told state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya on Wednesday that there was “no truth” to reports of troops moving towards the region. He said al-Zaidi was committed to “protecting the people of the region, not threatening them”. He added that the salaries of the Kurdish region’s public employees would be secured in the 2027 budget.

Baghdad is framing the measures as part of a wider drive to secure state security. Earlier this month, Iraqi forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad, a longtime stronghold of the Iran-aligned armed group Kataib Hezbollah. According to Reuters, the group allowed the forces in under a settlement brokered by politicians.

Abdulrazaq said al-Zaidi was justified “on the narrow facts”. “Oil smuggling across unofficial crossings is real and well-documented. However, smuggling is the pretext,” he said.

The security and defence consultant described the escalation as “largely a calculated domestic manoeuvre”. In Jurf al-Sakhar, al-Zaidi faces steep hurdles, he said. Rebuilding the town, returning Sunni Arab residents displaced for 12 years and fully expelling Kataib Hezbollah all risk triggering an intra-Shia clash.

“A controlled dispute with the Kurdistan Regional Government carries far lower political costs for Baghdad than an armed confrontation among Shia factions,” he said.

Al-Zaidi also needs to show his Shia coalition partners and armed factions that “he is decisive with everyone, not just selectively targeting some Shia militias”, Abdulrazaq added. He suggested a hard line towards the Kurds “may even have been an explicit demand from those factions” at the height of the Jurf al-Sakhar standoff.

Why are oil revenues so important?

Oil is the backbone of Iraq’s economy. It accounts for the overwhelming majority of state revenue and pays the salaries of millions of public employees, including those in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.

Baghdad claims smuggling is draining that wealth on a large scale. Al-Aboudi said tens of billions had gone into “private pockets and accounts” without benefiting the region’s residents. According to Al Jazeera’s al-Asa, the government estimates that 200,000 to 230,000 barrels of oil per day (bpd) are smuggled, worth about $200m a month.

Al-Asa has reported that oil is moved from the disputed provinces to other parts of Iraq and then abroad, or sent directly from Sulaimaniyah, Kirkuk and Erbil towards Iran. Most of the region’s unofficial crossings are on the Iranian border, he said.

The Iraqi News Agency has published excerpts from a government intelligence report which traces smuggling routes from Kirkuk and Sulaimaniyah to Iran and on to Afghanistan. The report also describes operations to disguise Iranian oil products so they can be passed off as Iraqi.

For Erbil, control of oil has been central to its autonomous status. In February 2022, the Federal Supreme Court ruled the region’s oil and gas law unconstitutional. The Kurdish region, which has enjoyed broad autonomy from Baghdad since the 1990s, has in the past ignored rulings by the federal court, and did so with that one.

The region’s independent exports suffered a major blow in March 2023 when the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline was halted after the International Chamber of Commerce in Paris ordered Turkiye to pay Iraq $1.5bn in damages over unauthorised crude oil exports from Iraq’s Kurdish region transported without Baghdad’s approval. Exports resumed in September 2025 under an interim deal between Iraq’s federal government, the KRG and foreign oil producers.

Revenue from border crossings matters, too. Salim Zakhour, a researcher in constitutional law and political systems who is based in Qatar, told Al Jazeera: “One of the key points of debate in the court’s decision is that it gave federal authorities oversight of revenues from non-oil fees and taxes, and I think this is one of the issues that could be contested in the court’s rulings.”

What has the Kurdistan Regional Government said?

The KRG has rejected Baghdad’s measures, calling them “a violation of the constitution and an infringement on the region’s rights”, and said it rejected “the language of threats” and a military approach to the dispute.

After a meeting on Wednesday, chaired by Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, the KRG’s Council of Ministers said it rejected “any attempt to return Iraq to a centralised system”. Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani said addressing the region in “military language” did “not solve any problem”.

Erbil has said it supports efforts to fight corruption and smuggling. It has called for the dispute to be settled through dialogue and full implementation of the constitution.

Opposition to Baghdad’s measures has spilled onto the streets. On Thursday, thousands of demonstrators gathered in Erbil, the capital of the semi-autonomous Kurdish region, protesting against the federal government’s move to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities. Erbil-based broadcaster Kurdistan24 reported that tens of thousands of people joined and that protesters were calling for Kurdish political unity.

The Kurdish news agency Rudaw reported that the region’s two main political parties, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), issued a joint statement that Baghdad’s decisions were “unexpected and deeply surprising”, warning that undermining the power of the Kurdish political entity is a “red line”.

But Abdulrazaq called the show of solidarity “a defensive reflex” driven by each party’s interests. A threat from Baghdad to one party is a threat to both, he said, and both risk losing the lucrative positions and budgets they have gained since the 2003 US-led invasion.

“It is therefore a pragmatic unity that will rapidly dissolve once the immediate threat recedes,” he said.

Where is this dispute headed?

For now, Baghdad appears eager to avoid any sort of military showdown. Abdulrazaq noted that the government has denied deploying troops to the region. It has also sent Popular Mobilisation Forces chief Faleh al-Fayyad to press Kurdish authorities for cooperation.

The legal ground has shifted in Baghdad’s favour. “The court’s decision is final and decisive,” the legal researcher Zakhour said. “But the issue is not only constitutional and legal. There is a political problem.” He said Erbil had been counting on challenging the measures in court, but al-Zaidi had “pre-empted this step”.

Outside support for Erbil also looks thin. Abdulrazaq said Washington is “heavily focused on supporting Zaidi”, particularly his agenda to consolidate state authority and rein in Iran-backed Shia armed groups.

“The Kurds should not expect American backing in this dispute; if anything, Erbil is more likely to face quiet US pressure to accommodate Baghdad’s demands,” he said.

Tehran, he said, is also clearly satisfied with the pressure on Erbil. Iran is angered by the presence of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in the region and has carried out drone strikes on their camps. Abdulrazaq stressed, however, that there is “no hard evidence” that Baghdad’s timing is part of a direct quid-pro-quo with Iran over Jurf al-Sakhar.

Ankara’s calculus is more pragmatic, he said, anchored in trade, energy and border security. Turkiye has little interest in an armed crisis on its southern border that could send more refugees across, and is likely to avoid overt intervention, he said. Instead, it will quietly favour an arrangement that keeps commerce stable and curbs smuggling.

What happens next?

In an effort to defuse the crisis, Iraq’s four presidencies have agreed to a proposal by Supreme Judicial Council head Faiq Zaidan to hold a national dialogue on December 1. The four presidencies are those of the republic, the government, parliament and the judiciary.

Abdulrazaq said the dialogue offered “a face-saving opportunity rather than a permanent fix”. He said it could lead to a temporary compromise, such as a joint oversight mechanism that polices official crossings while closing down unofficial ones.

“Long-term, however, the underlying tensions will remain in play,” he said. “The constitution is contradictory and Iraq doesn’t have a federal law that clearly delineates who is responsible for what in the oil and gas sector. These issues will simply resurface at a later date, even if both parties want to kick the can down the road.”
